This is a thread for people new to the project to say hi, ask beginner level questions, and get ideas of how to contribute to PhysLean.

If a conversation on a specific topic goes on for an extend amount of messages, it may be moved to its own dedicated thread - which is an equally good place to start. (Note that there is a general Lean channel for new members too, which can be found here - this thread is specific to PhysLean :)).

Hello everyone! I am recent graduate of bachelor's theoretical physics and I found this project very interesting to contribute. I hope that I will be useful addition to your community! I have a lot to learn from you guys!
Hi @Taewoo Lee ! What areas do you think you'd be interested in - or still exploring :)?
I have been skimmed through the TODO list and I am working on "lemma deriv_tanh"

Nice, so I think @Afiq Hatta is also working on this

  • #PhysLean > QM reflectionless potential @ 💬

but no harm in having two different solutions :). Ideally there should be a way to assign one self to a TODO-item, but I have yet to think of a good way of doing this.
yeah, we are working together now haha. I mean "physically."
we are sitting next to each other!
helping each other out
Perfect! :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:
I feel there are nothing much I can contribute after I read TODO list thoroughly, as I lack both physics and pure math skills, plus I only know numbers
@Taewoo Lee you have come farther than most , don't be discouraged, you did well today!!!

Hi @Taewoo Lee ,

As Afiq has said, you are really doing great!

Let me remark about the TODO items. The idea of the TODO items is that when someone is formalizing some area, they think of a result which would be nice to have but don't have the time to formalize it right there and then. A lot of them I wrote, and as such they are currently tilted to the stuff I have being formalizing. Given this, it is probably the norm rather than the exception for one to look at the TODO list and not find anything one is comfortable contributing too. This should be added to the fact that my writing is often quite poor (I have pretty badly dyslexia), and as such a lot of the TODO items are not as clear as they could be.
All that to say - don't be discouraged by the TODO list, as it only represents a very small subset of the ways one can contribute.

The projects ideas page contains another way to contribute - and this contains ideas from different areas and levels of physics. I appreciate that with these, there is something else scary about them, which is "where does one start" - but for a given project that is a great question to ask on the Zulip. There is also golfing and helping improve documentation :).

Let me finish with something generic: The apache software foundation (which is an organization that supports some open source projects) has a saying, called the Apache way, which says "community over code". That is building a great community is more important than building great code. This is something I stand very much by for PhysLean. The consequence being that I, and many others here, are very much willing to help new people join, give them advice, suggest ways to contribute etc. independent of their background or experience. At one point or another, we have all found formalizing physics or maths difficult - mainly because it is difficult, and if we can help someone else from what we have learned - even better :).

@Taewoo Lee, here is one potential way to contribute, which is something similar to what you and @Afiq Hatta where working on yesterday:

The proof of this result related to the 1d quantum harmonic oscillator could (I think) be golfed, that is made shorter by using better tactics or combining the ones that already exist.
@Joseph Tooby-Smith Thanks for kind word and advice. It really helps. I will try work on 1d quantum harmonic oscillator. Thank you so much :)

Let me post here that I've made two tutorials on how to contribute to PhysLean via:

  • informal lemmas and definitions: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f9kJyQs92TM
  • and module doc-strings: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EOYH1aJdnnM

I plan to make some more, in particular one on golfing.

Here is said tutorial on golfing proofs:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QL-mjkPQDHs

I got a university supplied computer, so made a tutorial on how to download Lean and PhysLean on a Mac (there was probably an easier way of doing this then waiting till I got a new PC, but alas):

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UvteqIDBj38

I have been going through this tutorial (Mathematics in Lean) and found it really helpful and minimal:
https://avigad.github.io/mathematics_in_lean/mathematics_in_lean.pdf
It's a succinct 200 page pdf with accompanying light GitHub repo with lots of exercises and solutions. Screenshots of TOC and a sample page are attached:

Screenshot_20260109_235546_Chrome.jpg

Screenshot_20260109_235559_Chrome.jpg
We even have a shortcut for it -- #mil

I've been messing around with YouTube shorts - since they seem pretty quick to make. Thought it was worth mentioning this one: https://www.youtube.com/shorts/V7YT3jK1mhk, on helping with the structure of PhysLean via the API graph.

Hi everyone!
I am new to lean (having done the Natural Number Game a few years ago and watched some of the more high-profile mathematics projects here as a casual observer) and interested in trying my hand at some formalization.
I had in mind to do the O(4) symmetry of the hydrogen atom which allows one to compute the spectrum (which to my knowledge is not yet in PhysLean). This approach avoids solving differential equations and special functions.

I see there has been some discussion last year about the Schroedinger equation and operators. What is the current status of angular momentum operators in particular? I think my first goal would be to define Lij=xipj−xjpiL_{ij} = x_ip_j - x_jp_iLij​=xi​pj​−xj​pi​ and prove some basic facts such as [Lij,f(r)]=0[L_{ij}, f(r)] = 0[Lij​,f(r)]=0 and [L2,Lij]=0[L^2, L_{ij}] = 0[L2,Lij​]=0.
Hi Gregory! I think this is a great place to start. I don't believe we currently have anything on the angular momentum operator, so starting here seems useful.

Hello! I've recently completed an MSc in theoretical physics and am interested in formalization. I was thinking of starting a new project with the goal of formalizing some of the key results in SUSY from Witten's papers, and wanted to start with the Witten Index. Just wondering about thoughts on this, thanks!

Hi @Rianna J ! Nice to meet you! I think something like this is totally feasible, though may require a fair amount of work and prerequisites, so I wouldn't expect this to be an easy endeavour.

The most similar thing we have to this currently in PhysLean is the derivation of Wick's theorem (see e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.07939). It maybe be possible to use some of the definitions in this for e.g. defining the Witten index.

I think for projects like this, (which is also relevant to @Gregory Loges's message above), it is important to think about what the generally useful data structures, definitions and results are and build around these. These can act as smaller useful milestones which can be e.g. contributed to PhysLean, on the way to your main goal.

Hello! My name is Zhidong Zuo, I am graduated from Imperial for BSc and MSc Theoretical Physics. I am also a big fan of Ai for physics!

I used AI to scan the current master branch for missing content (Please correct me if I am wrong). I plan to start with the two most basic missing parts to get familiar with Lean and physlean: Galilean transformations and Poisson brackets.

Once I’m comfortable, I’m very interested in pushing forward the following areas:
GR:
Christoffel/Levi-Civita connection pipeline, explicit covariant derivative machinery for GR physics, Riemann/Ricci/scalar curvature, geodesic equation, Einstein field equations with a cosmological constant, Schwarzschild solution.
QFT:
Klein–Gordon, Dirac, and Proca equation modules; explicit Fock space formalism; S-matrix/Dyson series pipeline; path integrals and generating functionals; renormalization and the renormalization group.
Particle physics:
Yang–Mills theory and non-abelian symmetries.

I hope to find a set of best practices for using AI to automatically translate into Lean.
Hi Zhidong, nice to see you on here! This sounds like a great starting point to me. Concerning the Galilean transformations there is this PhysLean#911 which might help specify the requirements

Hi everyone ! I’m a third-year pure math undergraduate, and I'm hoping to spend some time this summer learning the basics and contributing to Physlib as much as possible. I was kindly pointed to this thread to introduce myself and get the understanding of this ecosystem.

I’m a formalization beginner have completed some of the Natural Number Game and I'm currently starting with other resources as well.

My background is in pure math, plus some QM and Classical Mechanics (and I'm happy to dive deeper into the physics as needed).

Does anyone have a rough update on the current formalization progress for undergrad-level QM or Classical Mechanics within Physlib? I would like to know some specific files, theorems, or sub-topics in those areas that I can start with and get experience on.

Welcome Shashank! You can find the Classical mechanics files here: https://github.com/leanprover-community/physlib/tree/master/Physlib%2FClassicalMechanics

There are many topics here that have been convered. If you look into the folder named "Pendulum" here, it has three problems from Landau and Lifshitz that are richly commented but don't have code exactly because we wanted undergraduates to work this out.

Just like mathlib, Physlib has pages on all files. Here's one for one of those Landau n Lifshitz files:
https://physlib.io/docs/Physlib/ClassicalMechanics/Pendulum/CoplanarDoublePendulum.html

As for quantum mechanics, there are lots of files - check out the Quantum mechanics folder that has many results work out, especially this in quantum harmonic oscillator: https://github.com/leanprover-community/physlib/tree/master/Physlib%2FQuantumMechanics%2FOneDimension%2FHarmonicOscillator
Then there are some results on tight-binding chain here, David Tongs's notes were being formalized here and we were thinking of covering Bloch's theorem and Floquet matrix next as covered in his lectures: https://github.com/leanprover-community/physlib/tree/master/Physlib%2FCondensedMatter%2FTightBindingChain

And many QFT results in this folder: https://github.com/leanprover-community/physlib/tree/master/Physlib%2FQFT. There's a paper on Wick's theorem as well that walks you through the formalization process for Wick's theorem : https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.07939

You can find a big list of open problems here: https://physlib.io/TODOList
Hope this helps

To add to @Shlok Vaibhav 's answer here: We also have a number of number of open issues here which describe APIs and requirements that we want to build (some of the specifics are lacking in some of these though).
@Shlok Vaibhav Thank you for providing these resources. This surely helps and also provides me a reason to learn more physics :) @Joseph Tooby-Smith Thank you for your guidance and remark.

@Shashank Pandey , just a hint on one of the possible ways to get started with quick feedback loop: go through the files and documentation, figure out any improvement or a new result that you would like to see or maybe just find an open item that falls withing your coverage and then make a quick TODO on what configuration space/lemma/def scaffolding you would like to see and get a quick feedback from the author of the files or this channel before delving into the details

Hi everyone! I’m Pranav, an undergrad at IISER Pune interested in physics, and I’m new to Lean.

I’ve completed most of the Natural Number Game and want to start contributing. Could you suggest what I should focus on next—any resources, topics, or beginner-friendly parts of mathlib/PhysLean?

Thanks!
Hi Pranav, see some of @Shlok Vaibhav 's suggestions above. I would also take a look at the TODO list to see if anything there takes your fancy. There are also some project ideas here.
For something specific: This TODO item might be a good place to start. I attempted it here Physlib#1050, but it hit a merge conflict which I currently don't have time to fix.

@Joseph Tooby-Smith Hello, I am completely unfamilier with git, so the todo item you suggested seems confusing, I would like to do a toy project to get more familier with using LEAN, before I start contributing.

This is something that may help you on this front:

https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLQveF4ZJyPHrpTiKN8jbrJKfxDPBq49Hw&si=ne16RRFasn8nk3Sk

This is a tutorial series made by @Joseph Tooby-Smith that helps ramp up on the codebase part (in vscode ide). (I feel PhysLib is a software native project and it will be good to get familiar with git, which anyways is required these days for collaborative projects)

A simpler project to practice git on lean is Mathematics in Lean:

https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathematics_in_lean/mathematics_in_lean.pdf

You can try cloning their book from GitHub, try making changes and see how it works. Very minimal compared to PhysLib.

Hope this helps.
(I haven't answered your question directly though)

Hi, I'm a sw engineer, i worked doing firmware and SoC validation some years ago and worked as SRE for several companies

about a year ago I began using lean4 with chatgpt to have a formal way to describe reasonings and equations , my target was not to prove them but to use it along with latex as a sort of mathematically condensed representation for knowledge - reasonings, this was used mostly for my own musings about physics

on linkedin i contacted Leonardo de Moura, at some point he shared a link to PhysLean/Physlib ,
Im here because I honestly believe Physlib/Lean4 is important for the future of science and engineering
Hi @Jorge Garcia , nice! Do you have anything in mind you would like to work on?

On the Physlib website, I tried to check if there was anything like a unit test , system test infrastructure that I could leverage to test my own stuff (sounds silly due to lean4 nature but I would like to ask anyway , just in case im not aware of it )
idea is to be able to eventually, offer a Reviewer friendly PR for what i have on this repo :
https://github.com/jagg-ix/physlib/commits/entropic-physlib

hi @Joseph Tooby-Smith , thanks for replying ,
this has been generated using a combination of wolfram mathematica/chatgpt/claude/gemini and cross checks, i recently leave my job as an sre , partially to be able to work on this is an attempt to formalize a proof that Entropy Production drives temporal evolution

this raises many eyebrows (and it should) , this is not based on a theory I pulled from a hat
If i get some help to prepare a reviewer-friendly PR can provide references to all papers used (most important are Verlinde Entropic Gravity,Nagao- Nielsen Complex Action and Caticha's entropic time)

We have some guidelines on what we are looking for when reviewing PRs here, one of the most important points there is the comment about PR length. What we are also looking for is things built into the existing infrastructure, so that they can be more generally used. If you have any mainstream results as part of your fork which fit that criteria that is a good place to start.

got it, thanks a lot, i think i should look into style.html, does mainstream results means theorems that did not appear on journals ?

for example, one PR that may fall on that category would be a change I made to formally include 'information' as a dimension , this is basically used already on mainstream (bekenstein, hawking,etc)

adding it to : Physlib/Units/Dimension.lean
would mean we can have : Defined in the order ⟨length, time, mass, charge, temperature, information⟩.

on journals it's implicit and diffuse but within Physlib that can be used as a formal way to track the dimension of information content
Shannon entropy, bits, qubits as a primitive base, independent of thermodynamic temperature.

without it SI/ISQ basis cannot distinguish dimensionless ratios from dimensionless information measues
as analogy this would be akin to how boolean types formalize the concept of true/false and allows to reason about it

does mainstream results means theorems that did not appear on journals ?

Hard to define mainstream properly here - but yes in general it includes things that appear in reputable journals, books, or on the arXiv (excluding in the physics.gen-ph category).
got it, sorry I reply this late, thanks for the information and congrats for starting this project. :tada:

Hi all, I’m new to Lean 4 and formalization, but I’m very interested in contributing to PhysLib. I’m a mechanical engineer by training, so I’m most comfortable around classical mechanics and related physics, though I’m actively working on making that knowledge more mathematically rigorous. Hi @Nathaneal! Nice to have you here. This seems like a good place to start! As far as I am aware no one else is working in this direction currently.

Hello everyone, Im also new to physlib. I have recently worked on one PR to provide an alternative definition of FiniteHilbertSpace such that it is compatible with QuantumInfo.

I looked through existing topics and would be interested in working on documentations to also learn better coding practices in lean.

https://github.com/leanprover-community/physlib/blob/master/QuantumInfo/States/Pure/Braket.lean

Hi all, I'm new here. I posted something in new members recently so I won't repeat myself too much. I'm an experimental subatomic physicist working at the US-based Electron-Ion Collider (I'm in Canada myself), mainly interested in QCD and EW sector of the Standard Model.
Hi @Wouter Deconinck ! Nice to have you (and someone with your expertise) here :)! Your first PR looks great and thank you for following the AI-policy! I added some comments there.

Hi all! I’m new to Lean 4 and formalization, and I’m interested in contributing to PhysLib, especially around quantum many-body physics and AI-assisted formalization/proof tools. :grinning:

I have an undergraduate degree in software engineering and am currently a Ph.D. student in physics. Some topics I’d be particularly interested in are:

  1. Formalizing quantum lattice many-body systems, including spin/fermion models, topological order, and related phenomena.
  2. Investigating auto-formalization and AI-assisted reasoning frameworks.
  3. Integrating formalization tools to enhance agentic frameworks for numerics and verification. In parallel, we are developing quantum.harness⁠, an early-stage agentic framework for quantum many-body numerics, and I think formalization tools could be useful there.

I have some basic familiarity with Lean and have tried formalizing parts of a quantum thermodynamics paper⁠ using QuantumInfo. However, I’m not sure where best to start. :thinking: Since I use AI tools heavily, I’m concerned about producing verbose or non-idiomatic Lean code, so I’d appreciate guidance on style, conventions, and suitable entry points before making substantial contributions.

Hi @Huanhai Zhou, Nice to have you here.

Seeing anything in the quantum lattice many-body systems direction would be great!
In terms of starting formalising: Maybe the best place to start here is a simple example system (if there is one) in this area, and then generalise from there.

It might also be worth you writing an API-map for this area, an example is given here.

In terms of using AI and auto-formalisation. You might be interested/have ideas related to this discussion thread: #Physlib > AI tools . More generally, AI generated PRs are fine as long as you follow the AI-POLICY.md and the AGENTS.md. The most important part of this is that small PRs are better (and will often get merged a lot quicker) then large PRs.

Since a few weeks, we have been focusing on writing a library for reasoning about quantum gates and circuits. I've just left a post about it over at the quantum info channel: #Quantum information > Quantum Computing: Organizing the community.

While I have been reading the Mathlib and the QI channels for a long time now, I'm embarrassed to admit that I had somehow missed that there was a PhysLib channel. Well, I'm subscribed now. Happy to help, if there are some chores that need to be done.

Dear PhysLean community,

My name is Philip. My professional background is in software engineering and cybersecurity, with intermittent work in AI since the early 1990s.

I am using Lean as part of a broader research effort into AI-assisted formalisation and automated software development. One area I am particularly interested in is whether formal methods can help make AI-generated scientific and mathematical work more auditable, especially in teaching and research settings.

At the GitHub link below is my first attempted PhysLean contribution: closing an open sorry related to inequalities in quantum information theory, specifically the joint convexity of the Umegaki quantum relative entropy.

Before opening a PR, I would be grateful for feedback on whether this is an appropriate contribution, whether the proof style is acceptable, and whether there are any changes I should make to reduce reviewer burden.

Proof-Joint-convexity-of-the-Umegaki-quantum-relative-entropy

Kind regards,
Philip
A message was moved here from #Physlib > First PhysLean contribution: request for guidance before PR by Philip Haynes.

Hi Phillip!

Nice to meet you!
It might actually be easier for you to open a PR in the first instance, as it makes it easier to see the actual changes you are suggestion.

I'm guessing the proofs are in this file. These look good, although you may want to see if you can golf them a bit. There are lots of have statements, the number of which can probably be reduced.

Hi Joseph!

Nice to meet you too!.
I have refactored the proof, updated the informal validations (e.g. generate human proof from lean and compare to original) and had my first go at a PR - hopefully not making too many errors.

If I have over baked the refactor - please let me know.
Hey - added some quick comments on your PR - in general it looks good.

Joseph — thanks for the quick turnaround. I’ve addressed your suggestions, except for the first one. I think that change is a little large for this PR, but I’m happy to pick it up as a separate refactor PR.
@Philip Haynes See my one remaining comment there :).

@Joseph Tooby-Smith My inability to properly validate the first refactor of this work did not sit well with me. After investigating Lean’s metaprogramming environment, I developed a mechanism to refactor the code automatically, apply a specified coding standard, and demonstrate a one-to-one correspondence with the original proof.
As a secondary benefit, this also enables interactive querying of Lean environments, from which I have generated some initial visualisations.
I am now packaging the tooling to make it easier to use and expect to submit the refactor later this week. For review purposes, would you prefer to see the individual code transformations or only the final refactored result?
If possible would be good and interesting to be able to see the code transformations as e.g. individual commits, as this helps with review but if not possible the final refactor is fine

The initial step in processing is to construct a graph model of the code, and then it generates code back out levelled. The source files are used as a hint to provide traceability back to the original work. I was thinking of showing visualisation of before and after situation - but as part of a submission package. I will pop up a few versions so you can see what you like.
Nice! Am very interested to see.

Concerning the first part: We are not using Lean architect as of yet. Best place to look for style guide is probably:

https://github.com/leanprover-community/physlib/blob/master/docs/ReviewGuidelines.md

Concerning the error; It is a bit difficult to help without knowing the exact steps. But have you tried deleting the .lake directory and starting from there?

I've tried looking at some of the informal definitions on the TODO list but they seemed a bit beyond me to be honest. I know a little bit about metaprogramming if there's anything that needs doing on that front, and otherwise I'd be super happy to help in any way I can, even if it's something that's a bit monotonous.

Thank you so much for your help.
Fergus Munro

Hey Fergus :wave: ! From the meta-programming side one task which I think does need doing eventually is replacing the Linters for PhyslibAlpha with Lean linters instead of python linters (which is what they currently are), and also to generally improve them.

On the more monotonous side there is that task of helping golf proofs (making proofs shofter), as well as attempting to remove the:

set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false in

throughout the code (not sure how easy that task actually is).

Let me know if you have any problems or if e.g. the scope of these is too broad etc.
Sorry for a possibly silly question but does lake build always take >= 20 mins for PhysLib or is it just a first time build thing?

Hey @Charles Thomas - yep first time it should take a long time to build, as it builds every file in Physlib. After that it will be much quicker as it only builds the files you edited and those down-stream.

Hi Physlib community!

My name is Cameron, and I am starting a PhD position at the University of Bath under the supervision of @Joseph Tooby-Smith. I'm new to Lean and formalization, but have a background in mathematics and theoretical physics to help me along the way! Looking forward to working with and getting to know the community.

As an additional comment to my previous introduction, I'm looking to buy a new laptop to use during my studies. Does anyone have any recommendations for this? Or perhaps specifications to look out for/to avoid when running Lean? Thank you!

Hi @Cameron Lee excited to have you as a part of the community, what sort of math and physics are you interested in?

On the topic of laptop, I think generally the most important thing would be CPU performance (especially single core) and RAM. The choice of laptops can be a large can of worms, so often making a decision is harder than finding the right laptop :) (I am not a fan of macbooks but a good macbook pro will probably be more than enough)

Hi Cameron!

I'm by no means an expert on this but I recently upgraded to a new laptop in part to handle Lean better. Like Nathaneal said, I believe the CPU and RAM are the most important for Lean's performance. I've found I could make do with a 6GB RAM laptop but it was pretty slow. My desktop is 16GB RAM and does well for most Lean tasks, but my new laptop has 48GB RAM which gives a significant performance improvement, particularly when rebuilding or working on a large file. I'd say at minimum do 16GB, but if this is something you'll be doing a lot of it's worth investing in more if you can.

Battery life is also worth considering since Lean will drain the battery faster than typical usage. You also don't want to skimp on storage because having multiple repos means multiple copies of mathlib so it can take a surprising amount of space. It's not huge, but can add up faster than you think so don't go too small.
